tupaia#summary: The Polynesian scholar who accompanied James Cook and whose chart documented the geographical knowledge of the Polynesians.
tupaia#text: Tupaia was a high-ranking priest of the god ʻOro on Raʻiātea who fled to Tahiti after an attack from Bora Bora and became an adviser to the chiefs there. In 1769 he joined the Endeavour under James Cook and drew a chart of some 70 islands that shows the far-reaching knowledge of Polynesian navigators. In New Zealand he was able to communicate with the Māori because their languages were closely related, and he mediated in encounters. He died of illness in Batavia at the end of 1770.
abel-tasman#summary: The East India Company captain who was the first known European to reach Tasmania, New Zealand and Fiji, and who also visited Tonga.
abel-tasman#text: Tasman came from Lutjegast in the province of Groningen and entered the service of the Dutch East India Company in Batavia. On his voyage of 1642/43 he sighted Van Diemen's Land, today's Tasmania, and the west coast of New Zealand; in a bay at the northern end of the South Island a bloody clash with Māori prevented a landing. He then visited Tonga and Fiji. In 1644 he explored the northern coast of Australia. Because his voyages yielded no profitable trading opportunities, the Company considered them a failure; today Tasmania and the Tasman Sea bear his name. He died in Batavia in 1659.
james-cook#summary: The captain who charted large parts of the Pacific on three voyages, paving the way for the British colonization of Australia.
james-cook#text: Cook was born in Yorkshire, learned seamanship on colliers and became known as a Royal Navy cartographer in Newfoundland. Between 1768 and 1779 he led three Pacific voyages on which he circumnavigated New Zealand, charted the east coast of Australia and visited many islands. On 14 February 1779 he was killed at Kealakekua Bay in Hawaiʻi during a dispute with local people. In Britain he was long celebrated as a hero of science; for many people in Australia and the Pacific his name now stands for the beginning of colonization.
arthur-phillip#role: First governor of New South Wales
arthur-phillip#summary: The naval officer who led the First Fleet to Australia and built up the penal colony at Sydney.
arthur-phillip#text: Phillip, an experienced Royal Navy officer, led the eleven ships of the First Fleet to Australia in 1787/88 and founded the colony at Sydney Cove in January 1788. In its early years the settlement struggled with hunger until supplies arrived. Phillip sought a peaceful relationship with the Eora but had men such as Arabanoo and Bennelong captured in order to learn their language; when he was wounded by a spear at Manly in 1790, he forbade retaliation. In 1792 he returned to England in poor health, and he died there in 1814.
bennelong#role: Wangal man and intermediary in the early colony
bennelong#summary: The Aboriginal man who mediated between the Eora and the British colonists and travelled to England with Arthur Phillip.
bennelong#text: Bennelong belonged to the Wangal, an Eora group on Sydney Harbour. In November 1789 Governor Phillip had him captured; after escaping the following year, Bennelong sought contact of his own accord and became an important intermediary, for whom a hut was built on the harbour at the place now called Bennelong Point, the site of the Opera House. In 1792 he travelled with Phillip to England and returned in 1795. He then lived among his people again and died in 1813.
pemulwuy#summary: The Bidjigal man who for more than a decade led armed Aboriginal resistance against the colony at Sydney.
pemulwuy#text: Pemulwuy belonged to the Bidjigal in the area of today's western suburbs of Sydney. In 1790 he fatally wounded the governor's gamekeeper with a spear, and from 1792 he led raids on farms and livestock near Parramatta and on the Hawkesbury River. In 1797 he was badly wounded and captured during fighting at Parramatta but managed to escape. Governor King had him declared an outlaw in 1801; in 1802 he was shot, and his head was sent to Joseph Banks in England. Today he is regarded as a symbol of Aboriginal resistance.
kamehameha-i#role: Founder of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
kamehameha-i#summary: The chief who united the Hawaiian Islands into a kingdom through long wars.
kamehameha-i#text: Kamehameha came from the north of the island of Hawaiʻi; his year of birth is uncertain and is usually given as around 1758. As a young warrior he witnessed James Cook's visit and later made use of European weapons and advisers such as the sailors John Young and Isaac Davis. After his victory at Nuʻuanu in 1795 he ruled most of the islands, and in 1810 Kauaʻi also submitted. He promoted the sandalwood trade but retained the old religion and the kapu system. After his death in 1819 he was succeeded by his son Liholiho as Kamehameha II.
kaahumanu#role: Co-ruler (kuhina nui) of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
kaahumanu#summary: The most influential wife of Kamehameha I, who abolished the kapu system after his death and promoted Christianity.
kaahumanu#text: Kaʻahumanu came from a chiefly family of Maui and became the most influential wife of Kamehameha I. After his death in 1819 she announced that he had appointed her co-ruler, and as kuhina nui she wielded great power alongside the young kings Kamehameha II and III. In the same year she brought about the abolition of the kapu system. Later she turned to the American missionaries, was baptized in 1825 and issued laws based on Christian principles. She died in Honolulu in 1832.
liliuokalani#summary: The queen who was overthrown by American businessmen in 1893 and opposed the annexation of Hawaiʻi by the United States.
liliuokalani#text: Liliʻuokalani succeeded her brother Kalākaua on the throne in 1891. She sought to replace the constitution of 1887, which had curtailed the power of the crown and taken the vote from many Hawaiians, with a new one. American businessmen then overthrew her in January 1893 with the backing of US Marines. After a failed uprising by her supporters she was confined in the palace in 1895 and pressured into abdicating. She continued to fight against annexation, wrote her memoirs and many songs, including "Aloha ʻOe", and died in Honolulu in 1917.
hongi-hika#summary: The Māori chief who protected missionaries, travelled to England and led the most devastating campaigns of the Musket Wars.
hongi-hika#text: Hongi Hika was a rangatira of the Ngāpuhi in northern New Zealand. In 1814 he supported the founding of the first mission station, and in 1820 he travelled with the missionary Thomas Kendall to England, where he helped compile a grammar of the Māori language at Cambridge and met King George IV. On the return journey he acquired large numbers of muskets in Sydney. From 1821 he led great campaigns against tribes in the regions around Auckland, Rotorua and the Waikato. In 1827 he was wounded in battle, and he died in 1828.
william-hobson#summary: The British naval officer who negotiated the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 and became the first governor of the colony of New Zealand.
william-hobson#text: Hobson came from Waterford in Ireland and served in the Royal Navy. In 1837 he visited New Zealand and recommended measures to protect British interests; in 1839 he was instructed to obtain the consent of Māori chiefs to British rule. He had the Treaty of Waitangi drafted, which was signed on 6 February 1840, and in May 1840 proclaimed British sovereignty over all of New Zealand. He chose Auckland as the capital and in 1841 became governor of the new colony. He died in 1842 after several strokes.
george-tupou-i#summary: The ruler who united Tonga, gave it a constitution and preserved it from colonization.
george-tupou-i#text: Tāufaʻāhau was a chief from Haʻapai who was baptized by Methodist missionaries in 1831 and took the name George. He prevailed in the civil wars and in 1845 became ruler of all Tonga as Tuʻi Kanokupolu; the last Tuʻi Tonga lost his position. With law codes, the emancipation of commoners in 1862 and the constitution of 1875 he created a modern state, advised by the controversial missionary Shirley Baker. He reigned for almost five decades and died in 1893 at a great age.
edmund-barton#summary: The Sydney lawyer and politician who was one of the leading advocates of federation and became the first prime minister in 1901.
edmund-barton#text: Barton was born in Sydney, studied law and sat in the parliament of New South Wales. In the 1890s he campaigned tirelessly for the union of the colonies and led the work on the draft constitution. On 1 January 1901 he became the first prime minister of the Commonwealth of Australia; among other measures, his government passed the Immigration Restriction Act. In 1903 he moved to the new High Court of Australia as a judge, serving there until his death in 1920.
belisar#summary: Justinian's most successful general, who won back North Africa and large parts of Italy for the empire.
belisar#text: Belisarius came from the Balkans and rose as a young officer in Justinian's bodyguard. He fought against the Persians, helped to crush the Nika riots in 532, conquered the Vandal kingdom in 533/534 and from 535 large parts of Italy, including Rome and Ravenna. Because the emperor feared his fame, he was recalled several times; in 559 he saved Constantinople once more from an attack by the Kutrigurs. The later legend that he was blinded and died a beggar is considered unhistorical.
prokop-von-caesarea#summary: The most important historian of Justinian's age, who described his wars and buildings and, in a secret work, also his darker side.
prokop-von-caesarea#text: Procopius came from Caesarea in Palestine and accompanied Belisarius as an adviser on his campaigns against the Persians, Vandals and Ostrogoths. In his "Wars" he described these campaigns as an eyewitness, and in "Buildings" he praised Justinian's construction programme. In the "Secret History", which became known only after his death, he portrayed Justinian and Theodora in a hostile and spiteful way. His works are the main source for the period, but because of his shifting attitudes they need to be read critically.
herakleios#summary: The emperor who defeated the Persians but lost most of the East to the Arabs.
herakleios#text: Heraclius was the son of the governor of Carthage and overthrew Emperor Phocas in 610. He took over an empire that the Persians were overrunning from Syria to Egypt, reorganized the army and finances and defeated the Persians near Nineveh in 627. In 630 he brought the recovered True Cross to Jerusalem. A few years later, after the defeat at the Yarmuk in 636, he lost Syria and Palestine to the Arabs, who by shortly after his death had also conquered Egypt. During his reign Greek finally established itself as the language of the state, and basileus became the official imperial title.
leon-iii#summary: The emperor who defended Constantinople against the Arabs in 717/718 and set off the Iconoclast controversy.
leon-iii#text: Leo came from Germanikeia in the borderlands with Syria and took the throne as a general in 717, shortly before a huge Arab army and fleet laid siege to Constantinople. With Greek fire, strong walls and the help of the Bulgarians the city was saved in 718. Leo had the law newly summarized in the Ecloga and turned against the veneration of religious images. How far his measures against icons actually went is disputed, since the sources come almost entirely from his opponents.
irene-von-athen#summary: The first woman to rule the Byzantine Empire alone, and the restorer of the veneration of images.
irene-von-athen#text: Irene came from Athens and married Emperor Leo IV. After his death in 780 she ruled for her son Constantine VI and in 787 had the veneration of images restored at the Second Council of Nicaea. In a power struggle with her son she had him blinded in 797 and then ruled alone, calling herself basileus, emperor, in documents. In the West the imperial throne was therefore considered vacant, which was one of the justifications for the coronation of Charlemagne in 800. In 802 Irene was overthrown and died in exile on Lesbos.
kyrill#role: Scholar and Apostle to the Slavs
kyrill#summary: The scholar from Thessaloniki who created the first Slavic script and, with his brother Methodius, evangelized the Slavs.
kyrill#text: Cyril was originally called Constantine and took the name Cyril only as a monk shortly before his death. He studied in Constantinople, taught philosophy there and undertook diplomatic missions to the Arabs and the Khazars. From 863 he worked with his brother Methodius in Great Moravia, created the Glagolitic script and translated liturgical texts into Slavic. In 867 the brothers travelled to Rome, where Pope Adrian II approved the Slavic liturgy; Cyril died there in 869. The Cyrillic script bears his name but was developed only by his disciples.
method#role: Archbishop and Apostle to the Slavs
method#summary: Cyril's elder brother, who as archbishop built up the Slavic church in Moravia and Pannonia.
method#text: Methodius was at first an official in a province settled by Slavs and then became a monk. Together with Cyril he went to Great Moravia in 863; after his brother's death the pope consecrated him archbishop for Pannonia and Moravia. Frankish bishops who claimed the region for themselves had him imprisoned for several years. Until his death in 885 he and his disciples translated large parts of the Bible. Afterwards his disciples were driven out of Moravia and continued their work in Bulgaria. In 1980 Pope John Paul II declared Cyril and Methodius co-patrons of Europe.
basileios-ii#summary: The emperor who subjugated Bulgaria and brought the empire to the height of its medieval power.
basileios-ii#text: Basil II of the Macedonian dynasty became emperor in 976 and ruled for almost 50 years, longer than almost any other Byzantine ruler. In his early years he had to assert himself against powerful aristocrats; he was helped by Grand Prince Vladimir of Kyiv with an army from which the Varangian Guard emerged, and Vladimir received Basil's sister Anna as his wife in return. In decades of campaigning he defeated the Bulgarian tsar Samuel and incorporated Bulgaria into the empire by 1018. At his death the empire stretched from the Danube to Armenia and southern Italy, and the treasury was well filled.
alexios-i-komnenos#summary: The founder of the Komnenian dynasty, who stabilized the empire after Manzikert and asked the West for help.
alexios-i-komnenos#text: Alexios came to power in a coup in 1081, when the empire stood on the brink after the loss of Asia Minor and under Norman attack. He defeated the Normans and the Pechenegs, created a new stable gold coin, the hyperpyron, in 1092 and bound the great aristocratic families to the imperial house through marriage and titles. His request for military help contributed to the First Crusade, whose leaders he made swear to return conquered imperial territory. His daughter Anna Komnene described his life in the Alexiad.
anna-komnene#summary: The emperor's daughter who wrote the Alexiad, one of the most important historical works of the Middle Ages.
anna-komnene#text: Anna was the eldest daughter of Alexios I and received a thorough education in literature, philosophy and medicine. After her father's death in 1118 she is said to have tried to keep her brother John II from the throne in favour of her husband, and she afterwards withdrew to a convent. There she wrote the Alexiad, a history of her father's reign in elaborate Greek. The work is a principal source for the First Crusade and shows how alien and threatening the crusaders appeared to the Byzantines.
enrico-dandolo#summary: The aged, almost blind doge who steered the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople.
enrico-dandolo#text: Dandolo was elected Doge of Venice in 1192 at an advanced age and was by then almost blind. When the crusaders could not pay for the ships they had ordered, he took the cross himself and used the army first to capture Zara. He played a leading part in the expedition to Constantinople and the conquest of the city in 1204, after which Venice received important ports and a large quarter of the city. How deliberately he engineered the diversion of the crusade is disputed among historians. He died in Constantinople in 1205 and was buried in the Hagia Sophia.
michael-viii-palaiologos#summary: The emperor who recovered Constantinople in 1261 and founded the last Byzantine dynasty.
michael-viii-palaiologos#text: Michael Palaiologos came from an aristocratic family of the Empire of Nicaea and in 1259 became co-emperor of the child John IV Laskaris. After the recapture of Constantinople in 1261 he had the boy blinded and ruled alone, for which the patriarch excommunicated him. To avert an attack by Charles of Anjou he agreed to a union with Rome at the Council of Lyon in 1274, which met with fierce resistance in Byzantium. His diplomacy fended off the dangers from the West, but he neglected the eastern frontier in Asia Minor.
olga-von-kiew#role: Princess and regent of Kievan Rus
olga-von-kiew#summary: The widow of Prince Igor, who ruled the Rus for her son and was the first ruler of the Rus to adopt Christianity.
olga-von-kiew#text: Olga's origins are uncertain; the chronicle calls her the wife of Prince Igor of Kyiv, who was killed by the Drevlian tribe around 945 while collecting tribute. The chronicle tells at length how Olga took cruel revenge for her husband; the stories bear legendary features. As regent for her son Sviatoslav she fixed set places and amounts for the payment of dues. Around 957 she travelled to Constantinople, where Emperor Constantine VII received her, and was baptized. Her son remained a pagan, but her grandson Volodymyr introduced Christianity. The Orthodox Church venerates Olga as a saint.
wladimir-i#summary: The grand prince who accepted baptism in 988 and made Orthodox Christianity the religion of Kievan Rus.
wladimir-i#text: Volodymyr, known in Russian as Vladimir, was a son of Prince Sviatoslav and first ruled in Novgorod. With the help of Varangian warriors he conquered Kyiv around 978 and set up statues of pagan gods there, such as the thunder god Perun. In 988 he was baptized, married Anna, the sister of the Byzantine emperor Basil II, and had the people of Kyiv baptized in the Dnieper. He built the Church of the Tithes, brought priests and builders from Byzantium and protected the land against the steppe peoples with lines of fortifications. After his death in 1015 his sons fought over the succession. The Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint.
jaroslaw-der-weise#summary: The grand prince under whom Kyiv became one of the most splendid cities in Europe and the first law code of the Rus was created.
jaroslaw-der-weise#text: Yaroslav, a son of Volodymyr I, first ruled in Novgorod and after his father's death prevailed against his brother Sviatopolk; from 1019 to 1054 he was grand prince of Kyiv. He fortified Kyiv, built St Sophia's Cathedral and had books translated from Greek, and in 1051 he installed Hilarion as the first native-born metropolitan. The oldest version of the Russkaya Pravda law code goes back to him. His daughters married into royal houses: Anna became queen of France, Elisabeth queen of Norway and Anastasia queen of Hungary. His sarcophagus still stands in St Sophia's Cathedral in Kyiv.
alexander-newski#role: Prince of Novgorod and Grand Prince of Vladimir
alexander-newski#summary: The prince who fought off Swedes and crusading knights but submitted to the Golden Horde and later became a national hero.
alexander-newski#text: Alexander, son of Grand Prince Yaroslav II, became prince of Novgorod as a young man. In 1240 he defeated the Swedes on the Neva, and in 1242 the Livonian Order on Lake Peipus. Towards the Mongols he relied on cooperation: he travelled to the Horde several times, became grand prince of Vladimir in 1252 and helped enforce a census of the Horde in Novgorod against the resistance of its citizens. He died in 1263 on his way back from the Horde. The church canonized him in 1547, and Peter the Great had his remains brought to St Petersburg. Whether he was above all a defender or a vassal of the Mongols is judged differently.
dmitri-donskoi#role: Grand Prince of Moscow and Vladimir
dmitri-donskoi#summary: The grand prince of Moscow who defeated the Horde on the field of Kulikovo in 1380 and made Moscow the leading power of the Rus.
dmitri-donskoi#text: Dmitry became prince of Moscow at the age of nine; during his childhood Metropolitan Alexius effectively governed. In the 1360s he had the Kremlin fortified with walls of white limestone and prevailed against Tver and Lithuania. In 1380 he defeated the warlord Mamai on the Don, which gave him his byname, but in 1382 Khan Tokhtamysh devastated Moscow, and Dmitry had to pay tribute again. In his will he bequeathed the grand principality to his son Vasily as if it were a hereditary Muscovite possession. The Orthodox Church canonized him in 1988.
jogaila#role: Grand Duke of Lithuania and King of Poland
jogaila#summary: The Lithuanian grand duke who was baptized, became king of Poland and founded the Jagiellonian dynasty.
jogaila#text: Jogaila became grand duke of Lithuania in 1377, a realm that reached from the Baltic to the Black Sea. In the Union of Krewo in 1385 he committed himself to baptism and to marriage with Queen Jadwiga of Poland; in 1386 he was crowned king as Władysław II. He had the Lithuanians baptized, refounded the University of Kraków in 1400 and, together with his cousin Vytautas, defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald in 1410. He largely left Lithuania to Vytautas as grand duke. His descendants, the Jagiellonians, ruled Poland-Lithuania until 1572 and at times also Bohemia and Hungary.
iwan-iii#summary: The grand prince who united the Russian principalities around Moscow and ended the obligation to pay tribute to the Horde.
iwan-iii#text: Ivan III reigned from 1462 to 1505 and tripled the territory of Moscow: he subdued Novgorod, Tver and other principalities and called himself "sovereign of all Rus". In 1472 he married Sophia Palaiologina, a niece of the last Byzantine emperor, and adopted the double-headed eagle as his emblem. After the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480, Moscow paid no more tribute to the Horde. Under him Italian architects built the present Kremlin walls and the Cathedral of the Dormition, and in 1497 he issued a law code, the Sudebnik. He is regarded as the real founder of the Muscovite state.
iwan-iv#summary: The first crowned tsar, who conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and established a reign of terror with the oprichnina.
iwan-iv#text: Ivan became grand prince in 1533 at the age of three and was crowned tsar in 1547. In his early years he reformed law, army and administration and conquered Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556; the advance into Siberia also began under him. The long Livonian War for access to the Baltic, by contrast, ended in defeats. From 1565 he persecuted supposed traitors with the oprichnina, had thousands killed and in 1570 had Novgorod laid waste. In 1581, in a fit of rage, he struck and killed his eldest son Ivan. His byname Grozny means "the Formidable" or "the Awe-inspiring" rather than "the Terrible".
francysk-skaryna#role: Scholar, physician and printer from Polotsk
francysk-skaryna#summary: The humanist from Polotsk who printed biblical books in an East Slavic literary language and is regarded as the founder of Belarusian printing.
francysk-skaryna#text: Skaryna came from Polotsk in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, studied in Kraków and in 1512 received a doctorate in medicine in Padua. From 1517 to 1519 he printed a Psalter and other books of the Bible in Prague in a Ruthenian version of Church Slavonic, with his own prefaces and woodcuts. Around 1522 he set up a press in Vilnius, where a prayer book for travellers and the Acts of the Apostles were produced. He wanted people to be able to read Holy Scripture in a language they could understand. In Belarus he is regarded as the founder of printing and as a symbolic figure of national culture.
bohdan-chmelnyzkyj#summary: The Cossack leader who led an uprising against Poland-Lithuania in 1648 and founded the Ukrainian Hetmanate.
bohdan-chmelnyzkyj#text: Khmelnytsky was an educated officer of the registered Cossacks in the service of the Polish king. After a Polish nobleman had raided his estate and he had sought justice in vain, he fled to the Zaporozhian Cossacks in 1647 and became their hetman. Allied with the Crimean Tatars, he defeated the Polish armies in 1648 and established a Cossack state in Ukraine with its own administration. In 1654 at Pereiaslav he placed himself under the tsar. In Ukraine he is regarded as the founding father of a state of its own, in Jewish memory his name stands for the massacres of Jews during the uprising, and in Poland he was long seen as a rebel.
tadeusz-kosciuszko#role: Military engineer and leader of the 1794 uprising
tadeusz-kosciuszko#summary: The officer who fought in the American War of Independence and in 1794 led the uprising against the powers partitioning Poland-Lithuania.
tadeusz-kosciuszko#text: Kościuszko came from a family of lesser nobility in the region of Brest in present-day Belarus and trained as an officer in Warsaw and Paris. In the American War of Independence he planned fortifications at Saratoga and West Point. In 1794 he proclaimed the uprising against Russia and Prussia in Kraków, won at Racławice with the help of peasants armed with scythes, and promised the peasants relief from their burdens. In October he was wounded and captured at Maciejowice. He died in 1817 in Solothurn in Switzerland and is honoured in Poland, Lithuania, Belarus and the United States.
taras-schewtschenko#summary: The poet, born a serf, whose collection of poems "Kobzar" became the cornerstone of modern Ukrainian literature.
taras-schewtschenko#text: Shevchenko was born a serf in a village south of Kyiv. His artistic talent brought him to St Petersburg, where in 1838 artists and writers bought his freedom by raffling a portrait. In 1840 his collection "Kobzar" appeared, which celebrated the history of the Cossacks and the suffering of the peasants in the Ukrainian language. Because of his membership in a secret society and poems critical of the government, he was exiled in 1847 as a common soldier to the Kazakh steppe, forbidden to write or paint, and pardoned only in 1857. He died in St Petersburg in 1861 and was buried near Kaniv on the Dnieper.
alexander-ii#summary: The tsar of the great reforms, who abolished serfdom in 1861 and was killed by a bomb in 1881.
alexander-ii#text: Alexander II came to the throne in 1855 during the Crimean War. In 1861 he abolished serfdom, introduced independent courts with juries, local self-government in the zemstvos and universal military service, and relaxed censorship. At the same time he had the Polish January Uprising of 1863 crushed, banned Ukrainian printing in 1876 and expanded the empire in Central Asia and the Caucasus. In 1867 he sold Alaska to the United States. After several attempts on his life, a bomb thrown by the revolutionary group Narodnaya Volya killed him in St Petersburg on 1 March 1881 by the Julian calendar.
nikolaus-ii#summary: The last tsar, who clung to autocracy, had to concede a Duma in 1905 and abdicated in 1917.
